column2: In a two sample z test for p1 - p2 what does the standardized test statistic measure?
column3: It measures the raw difference so direction is known but not unusualness.
column4: It measures how many standard errors the observed difference is from 0 under H0.
column5: It measures the pooled proportion so both groups have one shared estimate.
column6: It measures the significance level so rejection can be decided without a p-value.

column2: Why is the hypothesized difference in the numerator usually 0 for this test?
column3: Because the sample proportions must always add to 1 in two group studies.
column4: Because the pooled proportion can only be computed when both samples are equal.
column5: Because z tests require parameter values that make both tails identical by default.
column6: Because H0 states no population difference so p1 - p2 equals 0 under the model.

column2: What does p-hat-c represent in this procedure?
column3: The combined proportion of successes from both samples treated as one sample.
column4: The average of p-hat1 and p-hat2 with equal weight regardless of sample size.
column5: The hypothesized success rate chosen from the alternative before data are seen.
column6: The observed difference p-hat1 - p-hat2 rewritten in proportion form.

column2: Why is the pooled proportion used in the standard error for this significance test?
column3: It reduces rounding error so the z statistic always has a larger magnitude.
column4: It matches the confidence interval method which always pools both samples.
column5: It reflects the H0 claim that the population proportions are equal.
column6: It forces each sample to have the same size before conditions are checked.

column2: A study asks whether treatment helps more than control. Which p-value tail matches Ha: p1 - p2 > 0?
column3: Use the left tail probability below the observed z value.
column4: Use the right tail probability at or above the observed z value.
column5: Use both tails and double the larger tail probability.
column6: Use the middle area between negative z and positive z.

column2: For Ha: p1 - p2 < 0 which p-value rule is correct?
column3: Use the right tail at or above the observed z value.
column4: Use both tails because any direction supports the claim.
column5: Use the absolute value of z and then double one tail.
column6: Use the left tail at or below the observed z value.

column2: For Ha: p1 - p2 != 0 how is the p-value determined?
column3: Find probability as extreme in either direction usually by doubling one tail.
column4: Find right tail probability only since z can be positive or negative.
column5: Find left tail probability only because differences are centered at zero.
column6: Find the probability between negative z and positive z around zero.

column2: Which statement best interprets a p-value in context?
column3: It is the chance the null is true after seeing the sample outcomes.
column4: It is the chance the alternative is false because the estimate was small.
column5: Assuming H0 is true it is the probability of evidence this extreme by chance.
column6: Assuming Ha is true it is the probability the sample difference equals zero.

column2: Which phrase must appear in a valid p-value interpretation?
column3: Given the observed sample difference we know which claim is correct.
column4: Assuming the null hypothesis is true for the population proportions.
column5: Given the alternative hypothesis is true for both populations.
column6: Assuming the significance level was chosen as 0.05 for the test.

column2: If p-value <= alpha what is the formal decision?
column3: Accept H0 and conclude both proportions are exactly equal.
column4: Fail to reject H0 because random chance still explains the data.
column5: Increase alpha and rerun the test until p-value becomes larger.
column6: Reject H0 and report convincing statistical evidence for Ha.

column2: If p-value > alpha which conclusion is appropriate?
column3: Fail to reject H0 and state the data are not convincing for Ha.
column4: Reject H0 and claim the population difference is exactly zero.
column5: Accept H0 and claim there is proof of no population difference.
column6: Reject Ha and conclude no future sample can show a difference.

column2: Why is fail to reject H0 preferred over accept H0?
column3: Because accepting H0 is only allowed when alpha equals 0.10.
column4: Because accepting H0 would ignore the pooled standard error formula.
column5: Because the test may lack evidence for Ha without proving H0 true.
column6: Because accepting H0 is only used for one sided alternatives.

column2: In this topic how should p1 and p2 be defined?
column3: As the sample proportions observed in group 1 and group 2.
column4: As true population proportions for the two groups being compared.
column5: As pooled success rates after combining all sample outcomes.
column6: As expected counts of successes under the null model.

column2: Which setup correctly names the inference procedure?
column3: One sample z test for a single population proportion.
column4: Two sample t test for a difference in population means.
column5: Chi square test for independence in a single contingency table.
column6: Two sample z test for a difference in population proportions.

column2: What condition must be checked before using this z procedure?
column3: Each sample is random or randomly assigned and groups are independent.
column4: The sample means are at least 10 standard deviations from zero.
column5: The pooled proportion is equal to each sample proportion exactly.
column6: The response variable in both groups is quantitative and symmetric.

column2: Why is the 10 percent condition checked for each sample?
column3: It guarantees the p-value will be small enough to reject H0.
column4: It guarantees pooled expected counts are whole numbers.
column5: It supports treating outcomes within each sample as approximately independent.
column6: It supports using a t distribution instead of the standard normal.

column2: Which count check matches the large counts condition for this test?
column3: n1*p-hat1 >= 10 and n2*p-hat2 >= 10 only for successes.
column4: n1*p-hat-c and n1*(1-p-hat-c) and n2*p-hat-c and n2*(1-p-hat-c) are all >= 10.
column5: n1+n2 >= 30 and both sample differences are within two standard errors.
column6: x1 and x2 must each exceed 10 while failures may be any size.

column2: A prompt asks whether a proportion changed over time with no direction. Which Ha fits?
column3: Ha: p1 - p2 > 0 because later results usually improve.
column4: Ha: p1 - p2 < 0 because earlier results set the baseline.
column5: Ha: p1 - p2 = 0 because no direction is specified.
column6: Ha: p1 - p2 != 0 because any change in either direction matters.

column2: When should the direction of subtraction p1 - p2 be chosen?
column3: Before data analysis so hypotheses and conclusion use one consistent direction.
column4: After seeing sample rates so the sign matches the larger sample proportion.
column5: After finding p-value so the wording matches reject or fail to reject.
column6: Before randomization so each group has identical sample sizes.

column2: Why should the final conclusion be written in context?
column3: Because formula symbols are not allowed after the p-value is reported.
column4: Because context prevents checking whether conditions were met.
column5: Because inference is about population claims not only symbolic statements.
column6: Because context changes the null from equality to strict inequality.

column2: If no significance level is given in this lesson what common default is used?
column3: Use alpha = 0.01 because z tests require a strict cutoff.
column4: Use alpha = 0.05 as a common standard unless another value is provided.
column5: Use alpha = p-hat-c because pooled data set the decision level.
column6: Use alpha = 0.50 so Type I and Type II errors are balanced.

column2: What does a small p-value indicate about the observed statistic under H0?
column3: It proves H0 is false for all possible samples from both populations.
column4: It means the pooled proportion was computed with the wrong formula.
column5: It means the estimate has no sampling variation under random chance.
column6: It means such extreme evidence would be unlikely from chance alone.

column2: What does a large p-value indicate in this testing framework?
column3: The observed statistic is reasonably plausible if H0 is true.
column4: The observed statistic proves the null is true in the population.
column5: The observed statistic guarantees equal proportions in future samples.
column6: The observed statistic must have come from biased sampling only.

column2: Which is a common misconception about p-values?
column3: They depend on the direction of the alternative hypothesis.
column4: They compare observed evidence to what H0 would generate.
column5: They are the probability that H0 is true after collecting data.
column6: They are computed from a standard normal model for z.

column2: Why can students build the test statistic formula from the AP formula sheet?
column3: Because the exact two proportion formula is printed in full on the sheet.
column4: Because the sheet gives the general test structure and needed standard error pieces.
column5: Because the sheet lists only calculator commands with no formulas.
column6: Because the sheet replaces p-hat-c with p-hat1 and p-hat2 by default.

column2: In a conclusion sentence which claim should be tied to statistical evidence?
column3: The sample proportions are fixed constants with no uncertainty.
column4: The pooled estimate equals the true difference in all populations.
column5: The null hypothesis has been accepted as certainly true.
column6: The alternative claim about population proportions is supported or not supported.

column2: Which statement about evidence and the observed difference is correct?
column3: A difference in the Ha direction is evidence but significance depends on chance under H0.
column4: Any nonzero sample difference automatically proves the alternative is true.
column5: A positive z value always implies reject H0 regardless of alpha.
column6: A negative z value always implies fail to reject for two sided tests.

column2: Why does a two sided test use extremeness in both tails?
column3: Because one tail gives the null area and the other gives sampling error.
column4: Because each tail corresponds to a different significance level.
column5: Because deviations above or below zero both support Ha: p1 - p2 != 0.
column6: Because the null requires twice the sample size for symmetry.

column2: Which statement correctly links random process wording in interpretations?
column3: Always say by chance alone in the random assignment even for surveys.
column4: Use random assignment for experiments and random samples for sample surveys.
column5: Use random samples only since experiments do not support inference.
column6: Use random chance wording only when the p-value is below alpha.

column2: Which ordering reflects a complete significance test workflow?
column3: State conclusion then check conditions then define hypotheses then compute z.
column4: Compute p-value then choose Ha then define parameters then name procedure.
column5: Check alpha then report p-value then create data from pooled model.
column6: State hypotheses and define parameters then verify conditions then compute and conclude.
